title: Valid Perfect Square
description: Brute force to optimized: linear incrementing versus binary search on the candidate square root, exploiting monotonicity.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer num, return true if it is a perfect square (there exists a positive integer k such that k times k equals num), without using any built-in library function like sqrt.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","num, a positive integer"],["Output","true if num is a perfect square, false otherwise"],["Goal","Determine perfect-square status without built-in sqrt functions, efficiently"],["Constraints","1 <= num <= 2^31 - 1"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Find an integer k such that k*k equals a target\", without using sqrt","Binary search on the candidate value k, exploiting that k*k grows monotonically"],["Large value range (up to about 2^31)","A linear scan of candidates would be too slow; binary search gives O(log num)"]]}

blocks.text: As k increases from 1 upward, k*k strictly increases as well. This monotonic relationship means a binary search over candidate k values can locate a match (or confirm none exists) far faster than testing every k from 1 upward.

blocks.title: Analogy: Guessing a Box's Volume by Guessing its Side Length
blocks.text: Picture trying to determine if a given volume could belong to a perfectly cubic (here, square) box, by guessing candidate side lengths. Since larger side lengths always give larger volumes, you can narrow your guess by half each time instead of trying every possible side length one by one.

blocks.caption: Since k*k grows monotonically with k, binary search directly applies to finding a matching k

blocks.text: Before testing every candidate k starting from 1, notice that k*k is a strictly increasing function of k, which is precisely the condition needed to apply binary search: narrow the range of possible k values by comparing mid*mid to num at each step.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If k*k equals num, k is exactly the value being searched for; if k*k is less than num, any valid k (if it exists) must be larger; if k*k is greater than num, any valid k must be smaller.

Observation 2: This three-way comparison is exactly the structure of a standard binary search, just applied to the candidate square root instead of directly to array elements.

Observation 3: The search range for k can start at [1, num], since for num >= 1, the true square root (if num is a perfect square) always lies within this range.

Observation 4: If the search range is exhausted (lo exceeds hi) without finding an exact match, num is not a perfect square.
This leads to binary searching over candidate k in [1, num], comparing mid*mid to num at each step, returning true immediately on an exact match, and false if the search range is exhausted.
Try k = 1, 2, 3, ... incrementally, stopping as soon as k*k reaches or exceeds num.

items: While k*k is less than num, increment k.
Once the loop stops, check whether k*k exactly equals num.

codes.python:
def is_perfect_square_brute(num):
    k = 1
    while k * k < num:                 # linear scan upward
        k += 1
    return k * k == num

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Incrementing k by 1 and checking k*k against num directly follows the definition of a perfect square.
This is correct, but for large num (up to about 2^31), the loop could run up to about 46,340 iterations, noticeably slower than a logarithmic search.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(sqrt(num)), incrementing k until k*k reaches num.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: since k*k is monotonic in k, binary search can locate the answer in O(log num) instead of O(sqrt(num)), a significant improvement for large num.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why linear incrementing is unnecessary: k*k as a function of k is strictly increasing, so testing a candidate mid and comparing mid*mid to num immediately reveals which half of the remaining range can be discarded.

How the search proceeds: maintain lo and hi bounds on the candidate k; at each step, compute mid, compare mid*mid to num, and narrow the range exactly as in standard binary search on a sorted sequence of squares.

Handling large num: using a 64-bit (or Python's arbitrary precision) integer type for mid*mid avoids overflow issues when num is near its upper constraint.

The core idea: binary search directly on the candidate k, using the monotonicity of k*k as the ordering.
Binary search with lo=1, hi=num. At each step, compute mid*mid; return true on an exact match, otherwise narrow the range based on whether mid*mid is less than or greater than num.

blocks.caption: Binary search directly on the candidate k, halving the range using mid*mid comparisons

blocks.text: Since k*k is strictly increasing as k increases, the standard binary search invariant holds perfectly: if mid*mid is less than num, every k <= mid is also too small, so the search can safely move past mid; if mid*mid exceeds num, every k >= mid is too large. This guarantees the search converges correctly to an exact match if one exists, or exhausts the range if num is not a perfect square.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log num), halving the search range each step.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: Valid Perfect Square is a clean example of applying binary search to a monotonic FUNCTION (k*k as a function of k) rather than to a literal sorted array, a technique often called "binary search on the answer."

items: Using a 32-bit integer type for mid*mid without care, risking overflow when num is near 2^31 - 1.
Forgetting num=1 is itself a perfect square (1*1=1), an edge case worth double-checking.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["num = 1","True, since 1*1 = 1."],["num is one less than a perfect square (e.g., 15)","False, correctly detected once the binary search range is exhausted without an exact match."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly naming this as "binary search on the answer" (searching over candidate k values rather than array indices) shows awareness of this reusable technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "determine a property without using a built-in math function", think: binary search on the candidate value itself, using monotonicity.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear increment approach runs in O(sqrt(num)) time; the binary search approach runs in O(log num) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer, exploiting the monotonicity of k*k as a function of k.
Core Idea: binary search candidate k values in [1, num], comparing mid*mid to num, narrowing the range until an exact match is found or the range is exhausted.
Time: O(sqrt(num)) for the linear approach, O(log num) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: binary search applies to any monotonic function of a candidate value, not just literal sorted arrays.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, accessible introduction to "binary search on the answer."
One line memory trick: binary search candidate k; mid*mid too small means go bigger, too big means go smaller.
